# Abstract

The rapid global expansion of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry has produced a
labor market in which annual compensation varies dramatically across roles, experience
levels, work arrangements, and firm sizes, yet the relative importance of these factors
remains poorly understood. Grounded in Human-Capital Theory (Becker, 1964) and Tournament
Theory (Lazear & Rosen, 1981), and building on the visual analytics investigation by
Karygulov and Gaso (2025) as the mother study, this paper employs formal inferential
methods to test and quantify the salary determinants documented in prior descriptive work.
The analysis draws on the *Global AI Job Market and Salary Trends 2025* Kaggle dataset
(Sajjad, 2025), a cross-sectional sample of 15,000 AI job postings with salaries
standardized to USD, and applies three complementary techniques: (1) descriptive
statistics and visualizations to characterize the distribution of salary across key
subgroups; (2) a one-way ANOVA to test whether mean salary differs significantly across
experience levels; and (3) a multiple linear regression model, estimated on a 70/30
train–test split, to isolate the independent effect of each predictor while controlling
for the others. Experience level emerges as the single strongest predictor, with salary
rising steeply from entry through executive levels, a pattern consistent with both
human-capital accumulation and tournament prize structures. Remote work ratio exerts a
small but statistically positive effect, and both company size and education requirement
contribute meaningfully to compensation. The final model achieves an adjusted
R$^2$ $\approx$ 0.64 and a test-set RMSE of approximately \$38,000 USD, indicating
that the included predictors capture roughly two-thirds of salary variance while
substantial heterogeneity attributable to unmeasured factors such as job location,
specific technical skill sets, and industry sector remains. These findings offer
actionable, data-driven guidance for job seekers calibrating salary expectations,
employers designing competitive compensation structures, and educators aligning curricula
with market demand in the AI sector.

\clearpage

# Chapter 1: Introduction

## Background of the Study

Artificial intelligence has gone from a small area of academic research to one of the
most important economic forces in the world. Between 2020 and 2025, global investment
in AI surpassed one trillion US dollars, and job postings that require AI skills grew
by more than 70% across major economies (World Economic Forum, 2023). This growth has
created a job market where salaries can vary enormously: a new data analyst and a
senior machine-learning engineer may both work in "AI," yet their pay can differ by
hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Several factors are believed to drive these salary differences. Experience level is
often cited as the most powerful factor in technology salaries, with AI skills alone
carrying a wage premium comparable to holding a PhD (Stephany et al., 2023).
Remote work, which became common after the COVID-19 pandemic, also plays a role:
tech workers are willing to forgo up to 25% of total compensation for remote flexibility,
and employers may offer slightly higher pay for remote roles to attract talent
(Cullen et al., 2025). Educational credentials signal specialized ability in AI roles
(Stephany et al., 2023), and company size also affects how much workers are paid
(Kline, 2024).

## Statement of the Problem

The main research question is: **Which factors (experience level, remote work ratio, company size, and education requirement) significantly predict annual salary (USD) in AI-related jobs?**

Sub-questions include:

1. How is `salary_usd` spread across different experience levels, employment types, and
   remote work arrangements?
2. What is the size and direction of each predictor's effect on salary?
3. How well does the regression model predict salary on data it has not seen before?

## Objectives of the Study

**General Objective:** To find the key factors that determine annual salary in the global AI job market and to build a predictive model that explains salary differences across experience levels, work arrangements, company sizes, and education requirements.

**Specific Objectives:**
1. To describe how `salary_usd` is distributed across key groups using descriptive statistics and visualizations.
2. To test whether average salary differs significantly across experience levels using a one-way ANOVA.
3. To build a multiple linear regression model for salary, check the model's assumptions, and evaluate how well it predicts on a test set.

## Hypotheses

- **H0:** There is no significant relationship between experience level, remote work ratio,
  company size, education requirement, and annual salary (USD) in AI-related jobs.
- **H1:** At least one of these factors (experience level, remote work ratio, company size, or education requirement) significantly affects annual salary (USD) in AI-related jobs.

## Significance of the Study

This study helps **job seekers** understand what salary to expect, **employers and HR teams**
set fair and competitive pay, **educators** design programs that match what the market needs,
and **policy makers** make decisions about workforce development based on real data.

## Scope and Limitations

This study uses the *Global AI Job Market and Salary Trends 2025* Kaggle dataset (Sajjad, 2025), which is
a snapshot of 15,000 AI job postings. All salaries are in USD; differences in the cost of
living across countries are not adjusted for. Because this is cross-sectional data (one
point in time), we cannot prove that any factor *causes* salary changes, only that they
are related. The dataset contains no missing values in its published form, so imputation is
demonstrated for completeness only.

\clearpage

# Chapter 2: Review of Related Literature

## Related Studies

This section reviews three key empirical studies that directly examine factors shaping
compensation in the AI labor market. The first serves as the primary mother study from
which this paper draws its core variables and inferential approach; the remaining two
provide supporting empirical context.

**Karygulov and Gaso (2025)** conducted a comprehensive
visual analytics investigation of the global AI job market using the *Global AI Job Market
and Salary Trends 2025* dataset, the same 15,000-record dataset (published on Kaggle by
Sajjad, 2025) used in the present study. Through univariate visualizations, bivariate comparisons, and interactive dashboards,
the authors identified four robust patterns: (1) experience level was the single most
influential variable, with salary rising steeply from entry through executive levels;
(2) remote roles offered marginally higher pay than equivalent in-office positions, and
roughly one-third of postings were fully remote; (3) research-intensive roles clustered at
the master's and PhD level while engineering roles showed greater credential flexibility;
and (4) large organizations consistently paid higher median salaries than small or
medium-sized firms. The present study extends this work by moving beyond description and
building formal inferential models (a one-way ANOVA and a multiple linear regression)
to test whether these patterns are statistically significant and to quantify each
predictor's independent effect size.

**Cullen, Pakzad-Hurson, and Perez-Truglia (2025)** conducted a field experiment with
1,396 US tech workers, collecting revealed-preference data on actual job offers and
acceptances between May 2023 and December 2024. Their central finding is that workers
are willing to forgo approximately 25% of total compensation for a position that is
otherwise identical but offers partial or full remote work, an estimate three to five
times larger than prior survey-based studies. Crucially, they also found that tech
employers offer slightly *more* pay for remote positions than equivalent in-office roles,
suggesting the market does not penalize location flexibility and may even reward it. This
directly informs the expected positive direction of the `remote_ratio` coefficient in the
present regression model.

**Kline (2024)** reviewed the extensive literature on firm wage differences in the
*Handbook of Labor Economics* and confirmed that high-wage firms are systematically
larger, more productive, and more sought after by workers. Using fixed-effects estimators
applied to large administrative datasets, the review documents that the firm-size wage
premium is robust across countries and time periods, and that larger firms tend to employ
more credentialed, higher-wage workers, a pattern consistent with both human-capital
sorting and monopsonistic wage-setting. This provides direct empirical grounding for
including `company_size` as a predictor in the present regression model and for
hypothesizing a positive coefficient.

\clearpage

## Related Literature

### Human-Capital Theory (Becker, 1964)

Human-capital theory provides the primary theoretical foundation for this study. First
formalized by Becker (1964), its central premise is that workers accumulate productive
capabilities through deliberate investments in formal education, on-the-job training, and
professional experience, and that wages in a competitive labor market are expected to
reflect this accumulated productivity. The theory distinguishes between *general* human
capital (skills transferable across employers, such as programming proficiency) and
*firm-specific* human capital, valuable only within a particular organization. A recent
comprehensive review by Deming and Silliman (2024) confirms that returns to human capital
remain robust across modern labor markets, while also noting that the value of
higher-order, experience-based skills has grown relative to formal credentials alone. This
is especially relevant in AI occupations, where Stephany et al. (2023) found that
demonstrated AI skills carry a wage premium of 16% (comparable to a PhD) while the
return to formal degrees in AI roles has declined, suggesting that applied experience now
matters more than credentials. This theory directly justifies why both `years_experience`
and `experience_level` are expected to show strong positive relationships with
`salary_usd`, and why `education_required` should also carry a salary premium.
Human-capital theory offers the broadest coverage of this study's predictors,
simultaneously accounting for the experience gradient, the education premium, and the
company-size effect, making it the single most important theoretical anchor for this paper.

### Tournament Theory (Lazear & Rosen, 1981)

Tournament theory, originally proposed by Lazear and Rosen (1981), explains why
compensation does not rise smoothly with seniority but instead increases dramatically at
the top levels of organizational hierarchies. The core argument is that senior and
executive compensation functions as a *prize* in an internal competition: by making
top-level pay disproportionately large, firms create powerful incentives for workers at
every lower level to exert maximum effort. The theory predicts a convex salary-seniority
curve: modest gains from entry to mid-level, larger gains from mid to senior, and a very
large jump to executive compensation. Contemporary empirical work continues to support
these predictions. Wang et al. (2022) found a significant inverted-U relationship between
the top-management pay gap and corporate performance across 733 listed firms, confirming
that a moderately large pay spread at senior levels incentivizes talent advancement. Kim
and Koo (2023) further demonstrated a negative effect of tournament incentives on
innovation risk-taking, suggesting that while steep pay gradients motivate competitive
effort, they can also shape how workers strategically allocate effort, a nuance directly
relevant to interpreting the large Executive-level salary premium observed in AI job market
data. Tournament theory uniquely explains the non-linearity of the experience–salary
relationship, and the expected outsized magnitude of the Executive coefficient in the OLS
regression is one of this study's key empirical expectations.

\clearpage

## Conceptual Framework

The figure below maps the expected relationships between the study's predictor variables
and the outcome variable `salary_usd`. Predictors are grouped by the theoretical
perspective that most directly motivates their inclusion: Human-Capital Theory (Becker,
1964) and Tournament Theory (Lazear & Rosen, 1981). Arrows marked with a "+" sign
indicate a hypothesized positive relationship supported by theory and prior research; the
"?" on employment type reflects the absence of a clear directional prediction.

```{r conceptual-framework, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5, fig.width=8.5, fig.align='center', out.width='80%'}
library(grid)

# Setup a clean viewport that fills the figure region
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(x = 0.5, y = 0.5, width = 0.95, height = 0.95,
                      just = c("centre", "centre"), clip = "off"))

# Colour palette
col_blue  <- "#2C6FAD"; fill_blue  <- "#D0E8F5"
col_green <- "#2E7D32"; fill_green <- "#D5EED5"
col_amber <- "#B06000"; fill_amber <- "#FFF0C8"
col_red   <- "#B02020"; fill_red   <- "#FADBD8"

# Helper: draw a labelled box
draw_box <- function(cx, cy, w, h, lines, fill, border, fs = 6.8) {
  grid.rect(x = cx, y = cy, width = w, height = h,
            default.units = "npc",
            gp = gpar(fill = fill, col = border, lwd = 1.1))
  n <- length(lines)
  for (i in seq_along(lines)) {
    off <- (i - (n + 1) / 2) * 0.028
    grid.text(lines[i], x = cx, y = cy + off, default.units = "npc",
              gp = gpar(fontsize = fs, col = "black"))
  }
}

# Helper: draw arrow with sign label
draw_arrow <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, lbl = "+", col = "grey30") {
  grid.lines(x = c(x0, x1), y = c(y0, y1), default.units = "npc",
             gp = gpar(col = col, lwd = 1.3, fill = col),
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "inches"), type = "closed"))
  mx <- (x0 + x1) / 2 + 0.012
  my <- (y0 + y1) / 2 + 0.010
  grid.text(lbl, x = mx, y = my, default.units = "npc",
            gp = gpar(fontsize = 7.5, col = col, fontface = "bold"))
}

# Helper: horizontal group label box (placed to the left of predictor boxes)
group_label <- function(cx, cy, label, citation, col, fill = "white") {
  grid.rect(x = cx, y = cy, width = 0.16, height = 0.045,
            default.units = "npc", gp = gpar(fill = fill, col = col, lwd = 1.2))
  grid.text(label, x = cx, y = cy + 0.012, default.units = "npc",
            gp = gpar(fontsize = 5.6, col = col, fontface = "bold"))
  grid.text(citation, x = cx, y = cy - 0.012, default.units = "npc",
            gp = gpar(fontsize = 5.2, col = col, fontface = "italic"))
}

# --- Layout constants - shifted right for perfect centering ----------
lx <- 0.38      # predictor box centre (was 0.35)
bw <- 0.30
bh <- 0.075

ox <- 0.72      # outcome box centre (was 0.75)
ow <- 0.22
oh <- 0.15

# --- Draw predictor boxes (left side) ---------------------------------
draw_box(lx, 0.82, bw, bh,
         c("experience_level", "(Entry / Mid / Senior / Executive)"),
         fill_blue, col_blue)
draw_box(lx, 0.70, bw, bh,
         c("years_experience", "(0 - 19 years)"),
         fill_blue, col_blue)
draw_box(lx, 0.58, bw, bh,
         c("education_required", "(Associate / Bachelor / Master / PhD)"),
         fill_blue, col_blue)
# Labels placed relative to the new lx
group_label(lx - 0.24, (0.82 + 0.58)/2,
            "Human Capital", "(Becker, 1964)", col_blue)

# Work-arrangement group (green)
draw_box(lx, 0.43, bw, bh,
         c("remote_ratio", "(0 / 50 / 100 %)"),
         fill_green, col_green)
draw_box(lx, 0.31, bw, bh,
         c("employment_type", "(FT / PT / CT / FL)"),
         fill_green, col_green)
group_label(lx - 0.24, (0.43 + 0.31)/2,
            "Work Arrangement", "(Cullen et al., 2025)", col_green)

# Organisational group (amber)
draw_box(lx, 0.16, bw, bh,
         c("company_size", "(Small / Medium / Large)"),
         fill_amber, col_amber)
group_label(lx - 0.24, 0.16,
            "Organisational Context", "(Kline, 2024)", col_amber)

# --- Draw outcome box (right side) ------------------------------------
draw_box(ox, 0.55, ow, oh,
         c("OUTCOME", "salary_usd", "(Annual USD)"),
         fill_red, col_red, fs = 7.5)

# --- Arrows from predictors to outcome --------------------------------
ax_start <- lx + bw/2 + 0.01
ax_end   <- ox - ow/2 - 0.005

draw_arrow(ax_start, 0.82, ax_end, 0.62, "+", col_blue)
draw_arrow(ax_start, 0.70, ax_end, 0.60, "+", col_blue)
draw_arrow(ax_start, 0.58, ax_end, 0.58, "+", col_blue)
draw_arrow(ax_start, 0.43, ax_end, 0.54, "+", col_green)
draw_arrow(ax_start, 0.31, ax_end, 0.52, "?", col_green)
draw_arrow(ax_start, 0.16, ax_end, 0.50, "+", col_amber)

# --- Footer note - centered with the whole figure ---------------------
grid.text(
  paste0("Theory: Human-Capital Theory (Becker, 1964; Deming & Silliman, 2024)  |  ",
         "Tournament Theory (Lazear & Rosen, 1981; Wang et al., 2022)"),
  x = 0.5, y = 0.02, default.units = "npc",
  gp = gpar(fontsize = 5.8, col = "grey40", fontface = "italic"))

popViewport()
```

*Figure 1. Conceptual framework showing the four predictor groups and their hypothesized
direction of effect on annual AI salary (USD). Arrows marked "+" indicate a positive
relationship supported by theory and prior research; "?" on employment_type reflects the
absence of a clear directional prediction. Note: employment_type is shown for completeness
but was excluded from the final regression model.*

# Chapter 3: Methodology

## Research Design

This study uses a **quantitative, non-experimental, correlational and predictive research
design**. No variables are changed or manipulated; instead, existing data are analyzed to
describe patterns and estimate salary prediction models. This design fits because: 
(a) it is
not possible to experimentally manipulate salary; 
(b) the research questions are about
prediction; and 
(c) the large sample size (n = 15,000) produces stable and reliable
estimates.

## Data Collection

```{r load-data, include=FALSE}
data_raw <- read.csv("~/Downloads/ai_job_dataset1.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
n_rows <- nrow(data_raw)
n_cols <- ncol(data_raw)
```

The dataset, *Global AI Job Market and Salary Trends 2025*, was downloaded from Kaggle
(Sajjad, 2025). It contains `r n_rows` records across `r n_cols` variables, with all salaries converted to USD. Table 1 provides a structured overview of all variables, their data types, and example values drawn from the first record.

```{r data-preview}
library(kableExtra)
var_overview <- data.frame(
  `#`       = 1:ncol(data_raw),
  Variable  = names(data_raw),
  Type      = sapply(data_raw, function(x) class(x)[1]),
  `Example Value` = sapply(data_raw, function(x) as.character(x[1])),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(var_overview, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Overview of all 20 variables in the AI job postings dataset. Each row describes one column in the raw data; the example value is taken from the first record. The outcome variable is salary\\_usd, already standardized to USD.",
      booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "scale_down"),
                font_size = 9,
                full_width = FALSE)
```

```{r imputation}
mode_val <- function(x) {
  ux <- unique(x[!is.na(x)])
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(x, ux)))]
}
data <- data_raw
num_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.numeric)]
for (col in num_cols) {
  if (any(is.na(data[[col]]))) {
    data[[col]][is.na(data[[col]])] <- mean(data[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  }
}
char_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.character)]
for (col in char_cols) {
  if (any(is.na(data[[col]]))) {
    data[[col]][is.na(data[[col]])] <- mode_val(data[[col]])
  }
}

na_remaining <- sum(is.na(data))
```

Following imputation, `r if(exists("na_remaining")) na_remaining else 0` missing values remained in the dataset, confirming that the procedure successfully resolved all detected gaps prior to analysis.

```{r factor-conversion}
data$experience_level   <- factor(data$experience_level,
                                   levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
                                   labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive"))
data$employment_type    <- factor(data$employment_type)
data$company_size       <- factor(data$company_size,
                                   levels = c("S", "M", "L"),
                                   labels = c("Small", "Medium", "Large"))
data$education_required <- factor(data$education_required,
                                   levels = c("Associate", "Bachelor", "Master", "PhD"))
data$remote_ratio       <- as.integer(data$remote_ratio)
```

\clearpage

## Variables Description

The **dependent variable** is `salary_usd`: annual gross pay in USD. Table 2 summarizes
each predictor variable, its measurement type, and its range of values.

| Variable | Type | Values / Range | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `experience_level` | Categorical (ordered) | Entry, Mid, Senior, Executive | Predictor |
| `years_experience` | Numeric | 0 -- 19 years | Predictor |
| `remote_ratio` | Numeric | 0, 50, or 100 (%) | Predictor |
| `company_size` | Categorical (ordered) | Small, Medium, Large | Predictor |
| `education_required` | Categorical (ordered) | Associate, Bachelor, Master, PhD | Predictor |

*Table 2. Study variables used as predictors of annual AI salary (USD). Categorical
variables were encoded as ordered factors prior to modeling; remote_ratio represents
the percentage of work performed remotely (0 = on-site, 50 = hybrid, 100 = fully remote).*

## Data Analysis Techniques

The following methods are used in this study:

1. **Descriptive Statistics**: Mean, median, standard deviation, frequency tables,
   histograms, and box plots to summarize and explore the data.
2. **One-Way ANOVA**: A statistical test to check whether average salary is significantly
   different across experience levels.
3. **Multiple Linear Regression**: A model that estimates how much each predictor affects
   salary, all at the same time, while holding the others constant. Includes assumption
   checks (VIF for multicollinearity, Breusch-Pagan test for unequal variance, residual
   plots for linearity and normality) and test-set evaluation using RMSE.

\clearpage

# Chapter 4: Results and Discussion

## Descriptive Statistics

The dataset contains 15,000 AI job postings. Table 3 summarizes the distribution of
annual salary (USD) across the full sample.

```{r desc-salary-stats}
sal_stats <- data %>%
  summarise(
    N      = n(),
    Mean   = round(mean(salary_usd), 0),
    Median = round(median(salary_usd), 0),
    SD     = round(sd(salary_usd), 0),
    Min    = min(salary_usd),
    Q1     = round(quantile(salary_usd, 0.25), 0),
    Q3     = round(quantile(salary_usd, 0.75), 0),
    Max    = max(salary_usd)
  )
kable(sal_stats,
      caption = "Summary statistics for annual salary (USD) across all 15,000 AI job postings. The mean exceeds the median, indicating a right-skewed distribution driven by high executive-level salaries.",
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The average annual salary is `r format(sal_stats$Mean, big.mark=",")` USD (median:
`r format(sal_stats$Median, big.mark=",")` USD; SD:
`r format(sal_stats$SD, big.mark=",")` USD), ranging from
`r format(sal_stats$Min, big.mark=",")` to `r format(sal_stats$Max, big.mark=",")`
USD. Because the mean exceeds the median, the distribution is right-skewed -- a small
number of high-paying executive roles pull the average upward.


Tables 4 to 8 present frequency counts for each categorical predictor. The four experience levels are approximately evenly distributed (~25% each), ensuring salary comparisons across groups are not distorted by unequal cell sizes.

```{r desc-freq-tables}
make_freq <- function(df, col) {
  df %>%
    count(!!sym(col), name = "Count") %>%
    mutate(Percent = round(Count / sum(Count) * 100, 1)) %>%
    rename(Level = !!sym(col))
}
kable(make_freq(data, "experience_level"),
      caption = "Frequency distribution of experience level. Levels are approximately balanced (~25% each), supporting valid between-group salary comparisons.")
kable(make_freq(data, "employment_type"),
      caption = "Frequency distribution of employment type. Full-time (FT) positions make up the substantial majority of postings.")
kable(make_freq(data, "company_size"),
      caption = "Frequency distribution of company size. Small, medium, and large firms are represented in roughly equal proportions.")
kable(make_freq(data, "education_required"),
      caption = "Frequency distribution of education requirement. Bachelor's and Master's degrees account for the largest shares of postings.")
kable(make_freq(data, "remote_ratio"),
      caption = "Frequency distribution of remote work ratio (%). Postings are evenly split across on-site (0%), hybrid (50%), and fully remote (100%) arrangements.")
```

```{r desc-salary-by-exp}
sal_exp <- data %>%
  group_by(experience_level) %>%
  summarise(
    N      = n(),
    Mean   = round(mean(salary_usd), 0),
    Median = round(median(salary_usd), 0),
    SD     = round(sd(salary_usd), 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
kable(sal_exp,
      caption = "Mean, median, and standard deviation of annual salary (USD) by experience level. Salary increases steadily from Entry to Executive, with the Executive tier showing the largest spread (SD), consistent with Tournament Theory.",
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

\clearpage

## Visualizations

The histogram in Figure 2 displays the overall salary distribution. Most postings cluster
between \$50,000 and \$200,000, with a long tail extending toward \$400,000 representing
high-paying executive and specialized roles.

```{r plot-histogram}
ggplot(data, aes(x = salary_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 50, fill = "#4e79a7", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_density(colour = "#e15759", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Annual Salary (USD)",
       x = "Annual Salary (USD)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

*Figure 2. Distribution of annual salary (USD) across 15,000 AI job postings. The red 
density curve confirms a right-skewed distribution; the long upper tail reflects the disproportionately high compensation of executive-level roles.*

\clearpage

The box plots in Figure 3 confirm a clear, monotonic salary progression across experience levels. Entry-level salaries cluster well below \$100,000, while Executive salaries typically exceed \$150,000. The widening interquartile range at higher levels reflects greater heterogeneity in senior AI roles, consistent with Tournament Theory.

```{r plot-boxplot}
ggplot(data, aes(x = experience_level, y = salary_usd, fill = experience_level)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.25, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Annual Salary by Experience Level",
       x = "Experience Level", y = "Annual Salary (USD)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

*Figure 3. Box plots of annual salary (USD) by experience level. Median salary increases monotonically with experience, and the spread widens at the Executive tier, reflecting
wide variation in senior AI compensation.*

\clearpage

titles indicate a well-diversified sample with no single dominant role.*

there is a small positive association between remote work ratio and salary. The salary
differences *between* groups are far larger than the within-group effect of remote ratio --
reinforcing experience level as the dominant predictor while confirming a consistent
marginal remote-work premium.

\clearpage

## One-Way ANOVA: Salary Across Experience Levels

Before building the regression model, a one-way ANOVA is used to test whether average salary is significantly different across the four experience levels. ANOVA asks: "Is it plausible that all groups have the same mean salary, or are the differences too large to be due to chance?"

```{r anova}
anova_model   <- aov(salary_usd ~ experience_level, data = data)
anova_summary <- summary(anova_model)

f_val       <- round(anova_summary[[1]]$`F value`[1], 2)
p_anova     <- anova_summary[[1]]$`Pr(>F)`[1]
p_anova_str <- ifelse(p_anova < 0.001, "< 0.001", round(p_anova, 4))

anova_tbl <- data.frame(
  Source    = c("Experience Level", "Residuals"),
  DF        = c(anova_summary[[1]]$Df[1], anova_summary[[1]]$Df[2]),
  `Sum Sq`  = c(round(anova_summary[[1]]$`Sum Sq`[1], 0),
                round(anova_summary[[1]]$`Sum Sq`[2], 0)),
  `Mean Sq` = c(round(anova_summary[[1]]$`Mean Sq`[1], 0),
                round(anova_summary[[1]]$`Mean Sq`[2], 0)),
  `F value` = c(f_val, NA),
  `p value` = c(p_anova_str, NA)
)
kable(anova_tbl, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "ANOVA results for salary differences across experience levels. The large F-statistic (p < 0.001) provides strong evidence that mean salary differs significantly between experience groups.",
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The ANOVA yields F = `r f_val` (p `r p_anova_str`), indicating a statistically
significant difference in average salary across experience levels. **H0 is rejected.**
To determine *which specific pairs* differ, Table 11 presents the Tukey HSD post-hoc
results.

```{r tukey-hsd}
tukey_res <- TukeyHSD(anova_model)$experience_level
tukey_tbl <- data.frame(
  Comparison  = rownames(tukey_res),
  Difference  = format(round(tukey_res[, "diff"], 0), big.mark = ","),
  Lower_95_CI = format(round(tukey_res[, "lwr"],  0), big.mark = ","),
  Upper_95_CI = format(round(tukey_res[, "upr"],  0), big.mark = ","),
  Adj_p_value = ifelse(tukey_res[, "p adj"] < 0.001, "< 0.001",
                       round(tukey_res[, "p adj"], 4))
)
kable(tukey_tbl, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Comparison", "Mean Diff (USD)", "Lower 95% CI (USD)",
                    "Upper 95% CI (USD)", "Adj. p-value"),
      caption = "Tukey HSD post-hoc pairwise comparisons of mean salary (USD) by experience level. All six pairs are statistically significant (adj. p < 0.001), confirming that each experience tier commands a distinctly different salary.",
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

All pairwise comparisons are statistically significant (all adjusted p-values < 0.001), confirming that every experience level pays a distinctly different average salary. The salary gap between Executive and Entry level is the largest, consistent with Tournament Theory's prediction of a disproportionately large reward at the top.

\clearpage

## Multiple Linear Regression

### Train/Test Split

The dataset is split into a **training set** (70%) used to fit the model and a **test set** (30%) used to evaluate prediction accuracy on unseen data.

```{r reg-split}
set.seed(123)
reg_idx   <- createDataPartition(data$salary_usd, p = 0.70, list = FALSE)
train_reg <- data[ reg_idx, ]
test_reg  <- data[-reg_idx, ]
```

The training set contains `r nrow(train_reg)` rows and the test set contains `r nrow(test_reg)` rows, reflecting a 70/30 partition of the full 15,000-record dataset.

### Model Fitting

The regression model is:

$$\text{salary\_usd} = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{experience\_level}) + \beta_2(\text{remote\_ratio}) + \beta_3(\text{company\_size}) + \beta_4(\text{education\_required}) + \varepsilon$$
Each $\beta$ (beta) coefficient tells us how much salary changes for a one-unit increase
in that predictor, while all other predictors stay the same. $\varepsilon$ is the error
term (the part of salary that the model cannot explain).

```{r ols-model}
ols     <- lm(salary_usd ~ experience_level + remote_ratio +
                company_size + education_required, data = train_reg)
ols_sum <- summary(ols)

rsq       <- round(ols_sum$r.squared,     3)
adj_rsq   <- round(ols_sum$adj.r.squared, 3)
f_stat    <- round(ols_sum$fstatistic[1], 2)
p_model   <- pf(ols_sum$fstatistic[1], ols_sum$fstatistic[2],
                ols_sum$fstatistic[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
p_mod_str <- ifelse(p_model < 0.001, "< 0.001", round(p_model, 4))

rmse_fn        <- function(actual, predicted) round(sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2)), 0)
rmse_train_ols <- rmse_fn(train_reg$salary_usd, predict(ols, train_reg))
rmse_test_ols  <- rmse_fn(test_reg$salary_usd,  predict(ols, test_reg))
```

Table 12 presents the estimated coefficients. Experience level dominates all other
predictors -- the Executive-level coefficient is the largest in absolute magnitude,
consistent with Tournament Theory. The intercept represents the baseline salary for an
Entry-level, fully on-site employee at a small company requiring an Associate degree.

```{r ols-coeff-table}
coef_df <- as.data.frame(coef(ols_sum))
coef_df$Variable <- rownames(coef_df)
coef_df <- coef_df %>%
  select(Variable, Estimate, `Std. Error`, `t value`, `Pr(>|t|)`) %>%
  mutate(
    Estimate     = round(Estimate, 1),
    `Std. Error` = round(`Std. Error`, 1),
    `t value`    = round(`t value`, 2),
    Sig          = case_when(
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.001 ~ "***",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.01  ~ "**",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.05  ~ "*",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE               ~ ""
    ),
    `Pr(>|t|)`   = round(`Pr(>|t|)`, 4)
  )
kable(coef_df, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "OLS regression coefficient estimates for annual salary (USD). Each estimate reflects the change in salary associated with that predictor, holding all others constant. Significance codes: *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05.",
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

\clearpage

### Assumption Checks

A linear regression model is only trustworthy if its four main assumptions hold. These
are checked below.

**1. No multicollinearity.** Predictors should not be too highly correlated with each other, assessed using the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF). Table 13 confirms all VIF values are well below the threshold of 5.

```{r vif}
kable(round(as.data.frame(vif(ols)), 3),
      caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) for each predictor in the OLS model. All values well below 5 confirm that multicollinearity is not a concern.")
```

**2. Homoscedasticity:** the spread of errors should be roughly the same across all predicted values. This is tested with the Breusch-Pagan test. A p-value above 0.05
means this assumption holds.

```{r bp-test}
bp <- bptest(ols)
bp_p_str <- ifelse(bp$p.value < 0.001, "< 0.001", round(bp$p.value, 4))
```

The Breusch-Pagan statistic is `r round(bp$statistic, 2)` with a p-value of `r bp_p_str`.

The test checks whether the spread of residuals is constant across all fitted values (homoscedasticity). 
A significant result (p < 0.05) indicates heteroscedasticity, unequal error variance, which is common with salary data that spans a very wide range. This does not invalidate the regression findings but means standard errors should be interpreted with some caution.

**3. Linearity and normality of residuals:** the residual plots below check whether the relationship between predictors and salary is roughly linear, and whether the errors follow a normal distribution.

```{r diagnostics-plots, fig.height=6, out.width="100%"}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(ols, which = 1:4, pch = 16, cex = 0.35, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.12))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

How to read each panel: the **Residuals vs Fitted** plot should show random scatter
around the horizontal line; the **Normal Q-Q** plot should have points tracking the
diagonal closely; the **Scale-Location** plot should show an approximately flat trend
line; and the **Residuals vs Leverage** plot highlights influential observations.

*Figure 6. Standard OLS diagnostic plots (2 x 2 panel) for the fitted salary regression
model. Some fanning in the Scale-Location plot is expected given the wide salary range;
the Q-Q plot assesses whether residuals are approximately normally distributed.*

\clearpage

### Model Performance

Table 14 summarizes key fit and predictive accuracy metrics. The near-identical training
and test RMSE values indicate the model generalizes well to unseen data without overfitting.

```{r performance-table}
kable(
  data.frame(
    Metric      = c("R-squared", "Adjusted R-squared", "RMSE (train)", "RMSE (test)"),
    Value       = c(rsq, adj_rsq,
                    format(rmse_train_ols, big.mark = ","),
                    format(rmse_test_ols,  big.mark = ","))
  ),
  caption = "OLS regression model performance metrics. R-squared and adjusted R-squared measure variance explained; RMSE (USD) measures average prediction error on the training and held-out test sets respectively.")
```

### Interpretation

The regression model is statistically significant overall (F = `r f_stat`, p `r p_mod_str`),
meaning the predictors together explain a meaningful amount of salary variance.
**H0 is rejected.** Specifically:

- **R-squared = `r rsq`**: The model explains about `r round(rsq * 100, 1)`% of the
  differences in salary across job postings.
- **Adjusted R-squared = `r adj_rsq`**: After adjusting for the number of predictors,
  the model still explains `r round(adj_rsq * 100, 1)`% of salary variance. This is the
  better number to report.
- **Experience level** has the largest coefficients, confirming it is the strongest
  predictor of salary, consistent with Stephany et al. (2023).
- **Remote ratio** shows a positive coefficient
  (`r round(coef(ols)["remote_ratio"], 2)` USD per percentage point), meaning jobs that
  allow more remote work tend to pay slightly more, consistent with Cullen et al. (2025).
- **Company size and education level** are also significant predictors (see Table 12).
- **RMSE (test) = `r format(rmse_test_ols, big.mark=",")`** USD: on average, the model's
  salary predictions are off by about `r format(rmse_test_ols, big.mark=",")` USD when
  applied to new data it has not seen before.
- All VIF values are below 5, confirming multicollinearity is not a problem (Table 13).

\clearpage

# Chapter 5: Conclusion and Recommendations

## Conclusion

This study analyzed salary data from 15,000 AI job postings to find out which factors
most affect how much workers in this field are paid. Key findings are:

1. **Experience level is the strongest predictor of salary.** The ANOVA (F = `r f_val`,
   p `r p_anova_str`) and the large regression coefficients both confirm that salary
   increases steadily from entry to executive level. **H0 is rejected.**
2. **Remote work ratio has a small but positive effect on salary**
   (`r round(coef(ols)["remote_ratio"], 2)` USD per percentage point), supporting the
   findings of Cullen et al. (2025).
3. **Education requirement and company size also significantly affect salary**, as shown
   in the OLS coefficient table (Table 12).
4. **The regression model explains about `r round(adj_rsq * 100, 1)`% of salary
   variance** (adjusted R$^2$ = `r adj_rsq`), with a test-set prediction error of
   about `r format(rmse_test_ols, big.mark=",")` USD.

These results are consistent with human-capital theory (Becker, 1964), which predicts
that workers who have invested more in education and experience will earn more. They are
further reinforced by tournament theory (Lazear & Rosen, 1981), which accounts for the
disproportionately large salary jump observed at the executive level, a pattern that
human-capital theory alone, with its smoother predicted return curve, cannot fully explain.

## Recommendations

**Job seekers.** Focus on gaining experience and targeting larger companies, which tend
to offer higher salaries. Seeking remote or hybrid roles may also come with a small
salary advantage.

**Employers and HR teams.** Use experience level and company size as the primary anchors
when setting salary bands. Offering remote work options may help attract candidates who
would otherwise go elsewhere.

**Educators.** Align course content with the skills found in high-salary job postings to
help graduates compete in the AI job market.

**Future research.** A follow-up study could use panel data collected over time to test
whether these relationships are causal. Adding more predictors (e.g., specific skills,
job location) could also improve the model's explanatory power.

\clearpage

## Appendix D: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing

```{r appendix-cleaning, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=68)}
# Imputation function (for demonstration -- no actual missing values in this dataset)
mode_val <- function(x) {
  ux <- unique(x[!is.na(x)])
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(x, ux)))]
}

data <- data_raw

# Fill missing numeric values with column mean
num_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.numeric)]
for (col in num_cols) {
  if (any(is.na(data[[col]]))) {
    data[[col]][is.na(data[[col]])] <- mean(data[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  }
}

# Fill missing character values with mode
char_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.character)]
for (col in char_cols) {
  if (any(is.na(data[[col]]))) {
    data[[col]][is.na(data[[col]])] <- mode_val(data[[col]])
  }
}

cat("Remaining NAs after imputation:", sum(is.na(data)), "\n")

# Factor conversion
data$experience_level   <- factor(data$experience_level,
                                   levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
                                   labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive"))
data$employment_type    <- factor(data$employment_type)
data$company_size       <- factor(data$company_size,
                                   levels = c("S", "M", "L"),
                                   labels = c("Small", "Medium", "Large"))
data$education_required <- factor(data$education_required,
                                   levels = c("Associate", "Bachelor", "Master", "PhD"))
data$remote_ratio       <- as.integer(data$remote_ratio)
```

```{r appendix-regression, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=68)}
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.001 ~ "***",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.01  ~ "**",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.05  ~ "*",
      `Pr(>|t|)` < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE               ~ ""
    ),
    `Pr(>|t|)` = round(`Pr(>|t|)`, 4)
  )
kable(coef_df, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "OLS regression coefficients (*** p<0.001, ** p<0.01, * p<0.05)",
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

# VIF
kable(round(as.data.frame(vif(ols)), 3),
      caption = "Variance Inflation Factors (VIF)")

# Breusch-Pagan test
bp <- bptest(ols)
cat("Breusch-Pagan statistic:", round(bp$statistic, 2),
    " | p-value:", round(bp$p.value, 4), "\n")

# Diagnostic plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(ols, which = 1:4, pch = 16, cex = 0.35, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.12))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Performance table
kable(
  data.frame(
    Metric = c("R-squared", "Adjusted R-squared", "RMSE (train)", "RMSE (test)"),
    Value  = c(rsq, adj_rsq,
               format(rmse_train_ols, big.mark = ","),
               format(rmse_test_ols,  big.mark = ","))
  ),
  caption = "Summary of OLS regression model performance (RMSE values in USD)"
)
```
